content: Self-testing for HIV can be an effective way to help individuals learn their HIV status. However, it is critical that self-testing remains a voluntary process. No individual should ever be coerced or forced into using an HIV self-test (HIVST) kit. Coercive or mandatory use of HIVST kits is not considered self-testing and should not be supported or encouraged. The World Health Organization (WHO) does not recommend the use of HIVST kits by parents or guardians to test infants or young children. This is because HIVST kits are not reliable for children under 18 months of age due to the potential presence of maternal antibodies in the infant’s system, which can lead to inaccurate results. Screening for acute HIV infection (AHI) is particularly important in the context of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) delivery. Identifying AHI through clinical signs, symptoms, and potential exposure is often a prerequisite for initiating PrEP, alongside an assessment for PEP in cases of recent high-risk HIV exposure. For some clients, additional HIV testing one month after starting PrEP may be necessary to confirm that AHI was not present at the time of PrEP initiation. Facility-based HIV self-testing (FB-HIVST) has been explored as a complementary approach to traditional facility-based HIV testing services. While it has not been universally implemented due to concerns about its potential to replace existing services, some programs have demonstrated its effectiveness, particularly in settings with suboptimal HIV testing coverage. In these programs, HIV testing uptake increased by 5% to 64% within three months of implementation. Offering self-test kits at facilities has also been found to be simpler, more cost-effective, and less resource-intensive than risk-based screening tools, which may miss critical opportunities for HIV testing. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many health programs adopted HIVST in facilities to maintain essential health services and improve health system efficiency amidst healthcare worker shortages. Given its benefits, including acceptability, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and the lack of reported harms, the WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) has recommended FB-HIVST as an additional approach to facility-based HIV testing. However, this recommendation is conditional due to the low certainty of available evidence and variability across different settings. Systematic reviews have shown that FB-HIVST may increase testing uptake, improve HIV positivity rates, and achieve comparable linkage to care as standard testing services. Clients often find FB-HIVST easier, more acceptable, and cost-effective, with no reported social harms or adverse events. For example, in Zimbabwe, an integrated model of HIV testing and treatment services, including HIVST, was introduced in family planning clinics. Between October 2020 and December 2022, 18,756 women accessed family planning services, with 7% diagnosed with HIV. HIVST kits were used both onsite and at home, with trained staff providing counseling and linkage to care. HIVST has also been used to support PrEP delivery. PrEP involves the use of antiretroviral drugs by HIV-negative individuals to reduce their risk of acquiring HIV. Despite its proven efficacy, access to PrEP remains limited due to barriers such as long wait times at health facilities, frequent visits for HIV testing and PrEP refills, and stigma associated with PrEP use. Differentiated PrEP delivery models, including the use of HIVST, can simplify PrEP delivery, increase convenience, and reduce opportunity costs for clients. HIVST can be used for PrEP initiation, re-initiation, and continuation, and has been shown to achieve similar levels of PrEP continuation and refill rates as standard testing services. A WHO modeling study found that HIVST-supported PrEP delivery results in few missed infections, minimal risk of drug resistance at the population level, and no significant increase in program costs. Both oral and blood-based self-tests have been found to be equally effective at the population level. HIVST can also be used to support PEP delivery, with self-testing after a non-reactive result allowing for immediate initiation of PEP or PrEP without additional testing. To successfully implement HIVST-supported PrEP delivery, strategies should focus on creating demand for PrEP, expanding access, simplifying initiation and continuation processes, and enhancing individuals’ ability to use PrEP effectively. HIVST can be offered in various ways, such as replacing quarterly provider-delivered testing, being used as needed based on individual risk, or being combined with clinic visits to increase testing frequency and promote effective PrEP use. Clear policies, standardized training, and quality assurance systems are essential for the successful delivery of HIV testing and self-testing services. Providers should be trained to support self-testers, address questions about the testing process, and provide linkage to care when needed. Offering a mix of testing approaches, including facility-based, community-based, and self-testing services, can maximize access and uptake, particularly for individuals at high ongoing risk of HIV. For example, in Vietnam, a web-based distribution model for HIVST kits was piloted to improve access to testing services for key populations. Clients could register online, request kits, and choose between home delivery or pick-up options. Reactive results were linked to further testing and care, while satisfaction surveys indicated high acceptability of the service. This model has since been scaled up to additional provinces, demonstrating its feasibility and potential for replication in similar settings. In conclusion, HIVST is a valuable tool for expanding access to HIV testing and prevention services. It is recommended as an additional approach to support PrEP scale-up and can be integrated into various service delivery models to meet the needs of diverse populations. However, ongoing research and operational studies are needed to optimize its implementation and ensure its effectiveness in different contexts.
